areas.purpose: Cool polished pregnant (green) liquor from ~98-104 degC to the precipitation fill temperature (72-78 degC for the agglomeration stage). The heat is recovered into cold spent liquor, which returns to A18 evaporation and liquor blending and from there to A06 digestion. A11 also holds the spent-liquor surge tank, a cooling-water trim cooler for tight control of the fill temperature, the cooled-PL split to agglomeration and seed repulping, and the hot-caustic clean-in-place (CIP) system for the exchangers. The temperature set here is the main lever on precipitation supersaturation, agglomeration and particle-size control.
areas.process_description: 1) Polished pregnant liquor (PL) arrives from the A10 security/polishing filtrate tank at 98-104 degC (aligned with A10). Typical composition is C ~240-255 g/L as Na2CO3, A/C 0.68-0.72 and suspended solids <10 mg/L. Four feed pumps (3 operating, 1 standby) send it through duplex basket strainers. 2) The PL passes counter-current through banks of gasketed plate heat exchangers (PHEs) against spent liquor from the A11 spent-liquor tank (55-62 degC). Six PHEs carry the duty and two are offline at any time for hot-caustic cleaning. The PL leaves at 76-82 degC and the spent liquor at 82-90 degC. The duty is ~80-100 MW for a PL flow of ~3,000-3,300 m3/h (engineering estimate: rho ~1.30 t/m3, cp ~3.2-3.3 kJ/kg.K, dT ~22-25 K; ~3.5-3.9 MW per K). 3) The regenerative PHEs cannot cool the PL below what the spent-liquor inlet temperature and approach allow. The rest of the cooling is done in a cooling-water trim cooler (1 operating + 1 standby), which sets the agglomeration fill temperature to ±0.5-1 degC. The fill temperature is a cascade master over both the trim-cooler cooling-water valve and a PL bypass valve around the trim cooler. 4) Downstream of the trim cooler the cooled-PL header splits three ways. About 2,000-2,600 m3/h goes to the A12 agglomeration distribution box. About 500-900 m3/h goes to the A13 coarse-seed repulp tanks. About 100-200 m3/h goes to the A13 fine-seed tank. Each split is flow-controlled; all values are engineering estimates. 5) Chemistry: as PL cools, the gibbsite equilibrium solubility A* falls steeply, so the liquor becomes supersaturated. Relative supersaturation is (A - A*)/C. Some gibbsite nucleates heterogeneously on the cooled PL-side plate surfaces, so the PL side of the PHEs scales with gibbsite in days. The spent side is undersaturated in gibbsite as it is heated and scales much more slowly, mainly with DSP (sodium aluminosilicate) and oxalate. Gibbsite scale is redissolved by circulating hot, strong, low-A/C liquor (A18 strong liquor, C ~300-320 g/L, A/C ~0.36-0.38, heated to 90-100 degC) for 2-6 h on a rotating schedule. 6) The heated spent liquor goes to A18 (evaporator feed and digestion-liquor blending; A18 owns the split between evaporation, ~1,700 m3/h, and the bypass to the blend tank). 7) Low-temperature (gibbsitic) and high-temperature (boehmitic) plants differ only slightly here. In a high-temperature plant the PL leaves the flash train and clarification at a similar ~100-106 degC, so the interchange duty is similar. Its higher digestion A/C (0.72-0.75+) gives a higher precipitation driving force. European high-caustic single-stage plants cool further (to a ~60-65 degC fill) to make floury or high-yield hydrate, and many older and high-temperature plants cool PL by multi-stage vacuum flash instead of PHEs.

equipment.working_principle: A centrifugal impeller adds velocity to the liquor and the volute converts it to pressure. The pumps run in parallel on a common discharge header, and the number running plus the VSD speed is set to hold the PL flow setpoint from the plant-wide liquor balance. Each pump has a minimum-flow recirculation line back to the source tank to avoid overheating at low flow. The liquor is near its atmospheric boiling point and near saturation, so suction pressure must stay above vapour pressure (NPSH margin) and dead legs must be avoided, because liquor cooling in stagnant pipe scales with gibbsite. Mechanical seals need a clean, compatible barrier or flush fluid (condensate) so caustic crystals do not form on the seal faces.

equipment.name: Pregnant liquor / spent liquor heat interchangers (regenerative PHEs)
equipment.function: Cool PL from 98-104 to 76-82 degC while heating spent liquor from 55-62 to 82-90 degC. This recovers ~80-100 MW that would otherwise be rejected to cooling towers.
equipment.type_selected: Large gasketed plate-and-frame heat exchangers (single-pass counter-current, 1-pass/1-pass, large-port plates ~2-3.5 m2 each), plates 316L SS, peroxide-cured EPDM clip-on gaskets; frame designed to ASME VIII Div 1 / PED
equipment.why_this_type: PHEs give a high U (thin turbulent channels) and close approach temperatures (~10-20 K) in a compact footprint, and they open for inspection. Cleaning by hot caustic recirculation is fast. A 2-of-8 standby allows continuous cleaning rotation. Large gasketed PHEs are a common choice for this duty in modern low-temperature refineries; SME to confirm. ALTERNATIVE: multi-stage vacuum flash cooling of PL (see 'alternatives').
equipment.alternatives: (a) Vacuum flash coolers: 4-6 flash vessels in series, each taking ~4-6 K off the PL. The flash vapour condenses in shell-and-tube spent-liquor heaters (or a barometric condenser on the last stage), and the last stages run under vacuum (~0.25-0.45 bar abs, allowing for the liquor boiling-point elevation of ~5-8 K). Advantages: no heat-transfer surface in contact with supersaturated PL, so no gibbsite fouling; the small evaporation (~1-3% of water) concentrates the liquor and slightly raises yield. Disadvantages: large vessels and vacuum systems, a poorer approach temperature, and condensate that must be recovered. It is widely used in older and high-temperature (European) plants and is a valid design choice. (b) Spiral heat exchangers: tolerate solids better but cost more per m2 at this scale. (c) Shell-and-tube: low U with viscous liquor, so very large. All values are engineering estimates.

equipment.working_principle: A PHE is a pack of thin corrugated stainless plates clamped between a fixed frame plate and a movable pressure plate by long tie bolts. Gaskets in each plate groove route the two liquors into alternate channels, so every plate has hot PL on one side and cold spent liquor on the other, flowing in opposite directions (counter-current). The chevron corrugations make the flow turbulent at low velocity, giving high heat-transfer coefficients and letting the outlet of one stream approach the inlet of the other closely. Because the PL becomes more supersaturated as it cools, gibbsite nucleates and grows on the PL-side plates, U falls and the pressure drop rises. The unit is therefore valved out, and hot strong liquor is circulated to dissolve the scale before the unit returns to service. Plate packs can be opened by sliding the pressure plate back along the carrying bar for inspection, gasket replacement or off-line high-pressure jetting.
details_to_model: Fixed frame plate (thick painted carbon steel, ~250 mm) with 4 corner nozzles (DN400-500): PL in at top and out at bottom, spent in at bottom and out at top (counter-current). Each nozzle has a flanged spool, a butterfly isolation valve with gear or actuator, and a flange guard
Movable pressure plate with roller hanging from the top carrying bar; bottom guide bar; 12-20 tie bolts (M48-M64) with nuts and bolt protection sleeves

Thermal relief valve on each side (discharging to the drain trench)

Frame painted carbon steel. Nozzle linings/sleeves 316L. Connected CS piping on the PL side and on the heated spent-liquor side (82-90 degC) has PWHT'd welds per NACE SP0403.

DSP or oxalate scale on the spent side (slow)

equipment.working_principle: An exchanger is first isolated on both sides and drained to the spent-liquor tank. Hot strong liquor is then circulated through the fouled PL side, often counter to normal flow, until the A/C rise in the return flattens, which shows the gibbsite has dissolved. The used solution, now enriched in alumina, is bled to the A18 digestion-liquor blend or to the spent-liquor tank so no caustic is lost, and the CIP tank is topped up with fresh strong liquor. The exchanger is flushed with spent liquor and returned to service. Some plants occasionally use an inhibited acid wash for stubborn DSP or oxalate scale; this needs a separate procedure and neutralisation.

areas.purpose: Crystallise gibbsite (Al(OH)3) from the cooled, supersaturated pregnant liquor onto recycled seed, in order to (a) recover alumina (yield ~75-85 g/L Al2O3, design ~80 g/L), (b) produce hydrate with the size distribution, strength and soda needed for sandy smelter-grade alumina, and (c) return spent liquor (A/C ~0.36-0.39) to the liquor circuit. Design: Australian-style two-stage process. A hot agglomeration stage with a low charge of fine seed is followed by a growth stage with a high charge of coarse seed and interstage cooling.
areas.process_description: Chemistry: Na+ + Al(OH)4- (aq) -> Al(OH)3 (s, gibbsite) + Na+ + OH-. This is the reverse of gibbsite digestion. It is slow and seeded, and is driven by supersaturation (A - A*), where A* is the gibbsite equilibrium solubility. A* falls with temperature and rises with caustic concentration (Rosenberg and Healy 1996 solubility model). The growth rate is roughly second order in supersaturation, with an activation energy of ~60 kJ/mol (Misra and White 1971). Crystallisation is exothermic: the heat of precipitation is of the order of 20-30 kJ/mol Al(OH)3 (engineering estimate, verify against the plant heat balance), i.e. ~25-35 MW at the design rate. Together with the required ~15-20 K fall in temperature, this heat is removed by the interstage coolers (45-70 MW) and by ambient losses from uninsulated tanks and launders (~15-30 MW, engineering estimate). Three mechanisms act together: (i) secondary nucleation creates new fine particles (<1-5 µm) and is favoured by low temperature and high supersaturation; (ii) agglomeration cements fine particles into ~20-60 µm agglomerates and is favoured by high temperature (>70 degC), high supersaturation and low seed surface area; (iii) growth deposits layers on existing surfaces and controls the yield. STEP 1, agglomeration stage (2 lines x 3 tanks): cooled PL at 72-78 degC from A11 (~2,000-2,600 m3/h, the balance of PL after the seed-repulp side-streams) is split equally to the two lines at a distribution box. Washed fine seed from A13 (fine seed charge ~30-80 g/L of agglomeration PL, engineering estimate) is added to tank AG-1. High supersaturation with little seed area promotes agglomeration of the fines into strong mosaic particles. Residence is ~7-11 h (engineering estimate, 5-6 tanks online, ~2,200-2,900 m3/h slurry). STEP 2, growth stage (2 lines x 13 tanks, 12 operating per line): coarse seed from A13 (filtered cake repulped in a PL side-stream; charge ~350-600 g/L on total PL, ~10-25 m2/L seed area, engineering estimate) enters G-1. Slurry flows through the tanks in series by bottom-draw airlifts and roof-level launders. Two interstage cooling stations per line (after G-4 and G-8) take the temperature from ~70-74 degC at G-1 to ~55-60 degC at G-13, maintaining supersaturation as A falls and maximising yield. Growth slurry flow is the total PL plus seed solids volume plus seed-cake liquor, ~3,700-4,400 m3/h (~1,850-2,200 m3/h per line). Through 24 operating growth tanks (~108,000 m3) this gives a growth residence of ~24-29 h, or ~23-28 h after an allowance for volume lost to wall scale. Total precipitation residence is ~31-38 h. CHANGE from the earlier draft: one growth tank per line was added (G-13), because 22 operating x 4,500 m3 gave only ~21-25 h once the seed volume was counted. The target spent A/C of 0.36-0.38 at this residence and end temperature must be confirmed with a precipitation model (open question). STEP 3: slurry from G-13 (A/C ~0.36-0.39, solids ~450-700 g/L on a liquor basis, ~33-40% w/w) gravitates to A13 classification. A crystal growth modifier (CGM, a surfactant/oil emulsion) may be dosed to suppress fines and coarsen the product. Precipitation needs no extra heat: the falling temperature profile is set by A11 and the interstage coolers. One tank per line is normally bypassed in rotation for descaling. Removed gibbsite scale is crushed at a scale pad and returned to A04 grinding/digestion, where it dissolves readily as high-grade, silica-free alumina. Contrast with European 'floury' or high-yield practice: higher caustic (~300 g/L), lower fill temperature (~60-65 degC), single stage, finer product. Boehmitic (high-temperature) plants use the same precipitation principles but can reach a higher PL A/C, so yield is higher for the same spent A/C.

equipment.working_principle: Each hydrofoil impeller works like a slow ship's propeller, pushing slurry down the tank axis. The flow turns at the floor, sweeps outward and up along the walls (the baffles stop the bulk from swirling), and returns to the impeller. This 'down-pumping' loop lifts settled particles off the floor (the just-suspended condition, Zwietering criterion) and circulates the whole volume several times per hour. Power draw is roughly ρ·Np·N³·D⁵, so small speed changes cause large power changes. The gearbox reduces the motor speed of ~1,480 rpm to ~10-18 rpm, and its output bearings carry the large downward thrust and bending moment of the long overhung shaft. Scale on the blades adds mass, unbalance and power, so torque and vibration trends show when a shaft needs cleaning.

areas.layout_notes: Precipitation is the largest tank farm in the refinery after residue. It has 32 tanks of ~14 m dia x ~31 m: 2 lines x (3 agglomeration + 13 growth). Each line is laid out as a 2-row serpentine (8 + 8 tanks) at ~18 m centres, so a row is ~145 m long, with a ~10-12 m aisle between rows carrying the roof-level launder gallery, pipe rack and stair towers. Lines A and B sit side by side, separated by a ~20-25 m access road for mobile cranes (~200-300 t class) and descaling equipment. The approximate block footprint is ~165 m x 130 m (engineering estimate). The interstage cooler stations sit at grade near G-4/G-5 and G-8/G-9 of each line. The compressor house is at one end, and the scale pad is at the block edge with truck access. The PL distribution box is on a steel tower or on the AG-1 roofs, fed from the A11 rack. Precipitation is upstream of (higher than) A13 so G-13 slurry gravitates to classification. Tank roofs are at ~31-33 m, and drives and bridges peak at ~36-38 m. Bunds (110% of the largest tank) have sumps at low corners. The precipitation cooling-tower block (A20) is placed nearby but downwind, to avoid drift onto the walkways.

A20 utilities: precipitation cooling water (A12 ~5,000-7,000 m3/h, 45-70 MW; the A20 tower must be sized for the combined A11 + A12 + A18 + A19 demand, ~14,000-15,000 m3/h), compressed air for airlifts (own compressors), instrument air, power (32 agitators x 90-160 kW plus pumps and compressors; area load ~6-10 MW, engineering estimate), condensate for seal and flush

areas.purpose: Separate the end-of-precipitation hydrate by size into (1) coarse product hydrate (to A14 filtration and A15 calcination), (2) coarse (growth) seed recycled to G-1, and (3) fine seed recycled to agglomeration after washing to remove co-precipitated sodium oxalate. A13 also recovers clear spent liquor (thickener overflow) for A11. Classification sets the product PSD and the seed balance.
areas.process_description: 1) G-13 slurry from each line (~1,850-2,200 m3/h, 450-700 g/L solids, 55-60 degC) flows by gravity launder into a primary cyclone feed tank (one per line). 2) Primary classification: slurry pumps feed a primary cyclone cluster. The cut size d50c is ~80-110 µm (engineering estimate), set so that the underflow solids rate equals the product rate (~370-420 t/h total). Underflow (coarsest particles, ~55-65% w/w solids) goes to the A14 product slurry tanks. Overflow goes to a secondary cyclone feed tank. 3) Secondary classification: secondary cyclones (finer cut, d50c ~40-60 µm, engineering estimate) produce an underflow of coarse seed (~1,050-1,800 t/h) and an overflow carrying fines (<~45 µm) and most of the liquor. 4) Coarse seed is dewatered on vacuum disc filters to remove spent liquor, which would otherwise dilute the supersaturation in growth. The cake is repulped with a cooled-PL side-stream (~500-900 m3/h from A11) in coarse seed repulp tanks and pumped to G-1. Because these tanks hold supersaturated PL in contact with a large seed area, they act as small precipitators and scale, so they are descaled on the same cycle as the precipitators. 5) Secondary overflow (~1,900-2,600 m3/h) goes to two tertiary (fine seed) thickeners. Clear overflow (spent liquor) gravitates to 11-TK-001. Thickened underflow (fine seed, ~400-700 g/L) is pumped to the fine seed drum filters. 6) Fine seed washing: on the drum filters the cake is washed with hot condensate (~85-95 degC). Sodium oxalate that co-precipitated on the fine seed during the cool end of precipitation dissolves, and the oxalate-rich wash filtrate goes to the A19 oxalate plant. This is critical in high-organic Darling-Range-type liquors and smaller for India East Coast bauxite. The washed fine seed is repulped with PL and pumped to AG-1. 7) Seed balance: if fines accumulate (nucleation event), excess fine seed can be sent to the product stream, returned to A06 digestion, or held in the fine seed tank. Classification therefore 'tunes' the PSD cycle. Alternative older design: three-stage gravity classifiers (primary, secondary and tertiary thickener/classifier vessels with rakes), still widely used.

equipment.working_principle: Slurry enters tangentially at high velocity and spins in the cylindrical section, creating a strong centrifugal field (hundreds of g). Coarse, heavy particles are thrown to the wall and spiral down the cone to the apex (underflow). Finer particles and most of the liquid move to the central upward vortex and leave through the vortex finder (overflow). The cut size is the particle size with a 50% chance of reaching either outlet. It depends on cyclone diameter, inlet pressure, slurry density and viscosity, and the vortex-finder and apex sizes. A 'roping' underflow means the apex is overloaded and coarse particles are being lost to the overflow; a 'spray' discharge is normal.

areas.layout_notes: A13 sits immediately downstream of (and at a lower grade than) the precipitation G-13 tanks, so slurry gravitates from G-13 via launders to the primary cyclone feed tanks. The classification building is a multi-level steel structure (~40 x 30 m, ~25-28 m high, engineering estimate). Grade holds the feed tanks, slurry pumps and repulp tanks. The seed filter floor (disc and drum filters) is at ~10-12 m, above the repulp tanks for gravity discharge. The primary and secondary cyclone decks are at ~18-22 m, above their feed tanks. Overhead cranes (10-20 t) serve the filter floor, and monorails serve the cyclones. The vacuum pump hall is at grade on one side. The two tertiary thickeners (~40 m dia) sit beside the building, higher than the spent-liquor tank (11-TK-001) so overflow gravitates to it. The A14 product filter building adjoins on the calcination side so primary underflow pipe runs are short. Floors are bunded and sloped to sumps, and safety showers are at every level.
interfaces: A12: G-13 slurry in; fine seed to AG-1; coarse seed to G-1
A11: cooled-PL side-streams for repulping; tertiary overflow and filtrates to spent-liquor tank 11-TK-001
A14: primary cyclone underflow (product hydrate slurry)
A19 oxalate plant: oxalate wash filtrate
A06 digestion: excess fine seed (if routed)
A07/A18: hot process condensate (wash)
A20 utilities: compressed air (snap blow), cooling water (vacuum pump seal coolers), flocculant, power; plant radiation-safety plan for nuclear density gauges

areas.purpose: Filter the product hydrate (primary cyclone underflow), wash out entrained spent liquor with hot condensate to minimise soluble soda carried to calcination and to recover caustic, and deliver a cake of ~6-10% free moisture to the A15 calciner hydrate storage at ~370-420 t/h dry. A14 also holds a product-hydrate slurry storage buffer so precipitation can keep running through a calciner outage.
areas.process_description: 1) Primary cyclone underflow (~55-65% w/w solids, ~185-210 t/h dry per line) enters the agitated product slurry tanks. 2) Filter feed pumps deliver slurry on a ring main to horizontal rotating table (pan) vacuum filters, 4 operating + 1 standby. 3) On each filter the cake forms in ~30-60 s, and the mother liquor (spent liquor) is drawn off to the mother-filtrate receiver and returned to 11-TK-001. 4) Two-stage counter-current displacement washing: hot condensate (85-95 degC) goes on the final wash zone, and that wash filtrate is recycled as the first wash. Weak wash filtrate returns to the liquor circuit (spent-liquor tank or residue washing, per the plant water balance). 5) The cake is dewatered by air drawn through it (dry zone), then discharged by a helical scroll to a collecting conveyor. A low-pressure air blow-back loosens the residual heel, and high-pressure sprays wash the cloth each revolution. 6) The cake (6-10% free moisture; soluble Na2O typically <0.05%, engineering estimate) travels by belt conveyor with a belt scale and automatic sampler to the A15 hydrate storage or calciner feed bins. 7) Buffer storage (added after review): when a calciner is down (each is 3,500 t/d nameplate against ~5,780 t/d plant rate) or the filters are down, surplus primary underflow is diverted to two large agitated product-hydrate storage tanks. These give ~3-5 days of buffer at the one-calciner deficit. The stored slurry is reclaimed to the filter feed tanks when calcining capacity returns. Total Na2O in the final SGA (~0.30-0.45%) is mostly occluded in the crystal lattice during precipitation and is not removed by washing; washing removes only surface liquor.

equipment.why_this_type: The horizontal cake allows excellent displacement washing with sharp separation of mother, wash and weak filtrates. It suits fast-draining, granular hydrate at high throughput, has a long industry record for product hydrate, and gives a clean continuous discharge.

equipment.working_principle: The table is a large horizontal ring divided into radial cells, each with a drainage grid and cloth and each piped to a central rotary valve beneath. As the table rotates, every cell passes through fixed zones set by the valve. (1) Feed: a feed box spreads slurry evenly and vacuum draws the mother liquor to the mother receiver. (2) First wash: recycled wash filtrate displaces the remaining mother liquor. (3) Final wash: hot condensate displaces the first-wash liquor; the wash filtrates are kept separate for counter-current reuse. (4) Dry zone: air pulled through drains the cake to 6-10% moisture. (5) Discharge: a slowly rotating helical scroll set a few mm above the cloth sweeps the cake radially outward over the rim into a chute, and a low-pressure blow-back through the valve lifts the heel. (6) Cloth wash: high-pressure sprays clean the cloth before the cell returns to the feed zone. Displacement washing works best with a level, crack-free cake, which is why the horizontal geometry is used.

areas.layout_notes: The product filter building (~60 x 30 m, ~20 m to eaves, engineering estimate) adjoins A13 and is as close as possible to the A15 hydrate storage and calciners, keeping conveyors short. Ground floor (0 m): product slurry tanks, feed pumps, filtrate receivers and pumps, the vacuum pump hall (acoustically separated) and the wash-water tank and heater. Filter floor (~6-8 m): 5 table filters in a row at ~16 m centres with hoods, and the feed and wash headers. Collecting conveyor 14-CV-001 runs under the filter discharge chutes at ~3-4 m, then turns onto an inclined transfer gallery to A15. A 20 t overhead crane covers the filter floor, with a ground-floor drop zone. The two product-hydrate storage tanks (~21 m dia x ~28 m) stand outside the building in their own bund between A13 and A14, with the reclaim pump bay beside them. The building is open-sided or louvred for ventilation, floors are bunded and sloped to sumps, and safety showers are at each floor and stair.

decisions.finding: A12 residence time ignores seed slurry volume (growth ~21-25 h, total ~28-32 h, not 25-30 / 32-38 h)

Agglomeration residence was also recalculated (~7-11 h), because ~600-1,100 m3/h of PL is now shown going to seed repulping. decisions.reason: PL at 98-104 degC and ~14 wt% NaOH-equivalent is in the PWHT region. Applied plant-wide philosophy to A11 (PL piping and strainers, heated spent-liquor piping at 82-90 degC, CIP system). Extended to nozzle/attachment welds (stress-relieved insert plates) on AG-1..3, G-1..G-4 and the coarse-seed repulp tanks (72-78 degC, at or near the line). Spent liquor <62 degC, cool growth tanks and hydrate storage are excluded. The chart check against the current NACE edition remains for the materials owner.

decisions.finding: Precipitator bottom strake 28-32 mm overstated; wide-gap PHE slurry velocity 0.3-0.6 m/s too low
decisions.reason: Shell: accepted in substance. Using API 650 Sd = 173 MPa for A516-70 (the reviewer used 160 MPa, which is the value for a lower grade), td = 4.9 x 14 x 30.7 x 1.55/173 + 3 ≈ 22 mm and tt ≈ 11 mm, so the bottom strake is now ~22-26 mm. The top strake is ~8-10 mm; the API 650 minimum for D <15 m is 5 mm, not 6 mm. Velocity: accepted that 0.3-0.6 m/s is too low. The design is set to 0.6-1.0 m/s (minimum ~0.5 with low-flow trip and automatic liquor flush) rather than 0.8-1.2 m/s. A check calculation (~35-50 slurry channels per unit, ~150-250 m2) shows 0.6-1.0 m/s fits the required area in single pass, whereas 0.8-1.2 m/s would force fewer channels or multi-pass with higher dP. Unit area and pump head were updated accordingly.

decisions.reason: Replaced with the reviewer's wording: bypass via launder gates, keep the agitator running until the level is below the lower impeller, never stop agitation on a tank holding slurry, and never open bottom doors until the tank is empty and washed. The same logic was applied to the emptying-pump description.

open_questions: STATUS (in reply to the user's 'what is the current status?'): Heat interchange (A11), precipitation (A12), classification (A13) and hydrate filtration (A14) have now been reconciled with the expert review.
